summary: This document describes uniform patterns for building HTTP URLs to retrieve registration information from Regional Internet Registries and Domain Name Registries, using RESTful web access. These patterns define the query syntax of the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP). It obsoletes RFC 7482.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9082 defines how a client writes an RDAP query as an HTTP URL. It covers lookups and searches for registered networks, numbers, domains, nameservers, and entities.

subtitle: URL path patterns for looking up registration information through RDAP.

tldr.problem: WHOIS services lack a common query structure and consistent response and error formats across registries.
tldr.mechanism: RDAP clients append a defined path segment or search expression to a service base URL and send an HTTP GET or HEAD request.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9082 is an Internet Standard that replaces RFC 7482. It defines query URLs; RFC 9083 defines RDAP JSON responses.

sections.title: The RDAP Query Format
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) uses HTTP URLs to query registration information from Regional Internet Registries and Domain Name Registries. RFC 9082 standardizes query patterns to address shortcomings of WHOIS, including a lack of common commands, output formats, and error structures.

The patterns cover queries for IP networks, Autonomous System numbers, domains, nameservers, and entities such as contacts or registrars. They apply to HTTP GET and HEAD; changing or provisioning registration data is outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: RDAP gives registries a shared way to express registration-data lookups in URLs. This RFC defines how to ask for information, not how the server formats its answer.

sections.title: Exact-Match Lookup Paths
sections.content:
A client obtains a service base URL and appends a path for the item it wants to look up. The path begins with a type such as ip, autnum, domain, nameserver, entity, or help.

An IP query can contain an address or a CIDR block and returns the most specific network that completely contains it. Other lookup paths identify an Autonomous System number, domain name, nameserver host name, or provider-specific entity handle. A HEAD request can check whether an object exists without requesting RDAP-encoded results.
sections.plainLanguage: The first path segment tells the server what kind of record the client wants. The rest of the path identifies the address, number, name, or handle to look up.

sections.title: Search Paths and Partial Matching
sections.content:
Search uses plural path names such as domains, nameservers, and entities, followed by one query parameter. Search fields include a domain name, nameserver name or address, entity name, or entity handle.

An asterisk matches zero or more trailing characters. A search string must not contain more than one asterisk. If a server supports the search feature but not the requested partial-match style, it should return HTTP 422 unless another status is more appropriate under its policy.
sections.plainLanguage: A search URL names the record type and one field to match. An asterisk can stand for a trailing part of a value, but each search may contain only one.

sections.title: Internationalized Names and Encoding
sections.content:
Internationalized domain-name labels may be submitted in Unicode U-label form or ASCII A-label form. An IDN should not mix those forms within one name, although a server may convert a mixed query or refuse it.

For non-ASCII query text, a client converts the text to UTF-8, normalizes it using NFC, and percent-encodes it for the URL. If the server finds invalid UTF-8 after decoding, it can return HTTP 400. DNS names are matched label by label; other strings use NFKC normalization with case folding for comparisons.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients can submit internationalized names in Unicode or ASCII form. They encode non-ASCII text as UTF-8 and percent-encode it before placing it in a URL.

sections.title: Adding Custom Query Paths
sections.content:
RFC 9082 defines common query paths but does not cover every object that every registry may expose. A custom path segment can be prefixed with a unique identifier and an underscore, which keeps it distinct from standard segments.

A server must return an appropriate failure status for an unrecognized path segment. Future IETF specifications may define additional query patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: Registries can define query paths for information types this RFC does not cover. A unique prefix distinguishes a custom path from standard RDAP paths.

sections.title: Search Limits and Privacy
sections.content:
Searches can use more server resources than exact lookups, increasing the risk of resource exhaustion. Operators can restrict search to identified and authorized clients, rate-limit requests, and limit the amount of information returned.

Search results may reveal relationships that an exact lookup would not show, including related internationalized domain names. Servers may vary the breadth of returned information according to client identity and authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: Broad searches can consume server resources and reveal links between records. A server can restrict who searches and limit the size of its results.
